public_rationale: This is an open-ended 'never' forecast. Read fairly, it says the models themselves cannot learn from experience and revise what they know, as people do, and never will. External memory systems wrapped around a frozen model do not count. No deadline exists, so it can only be settled early by a decisive refutation. MIT's SEAL framework (2025) showed an LLM generating its own finetuning data and making persistent weight updates. Its authors call this 'a promising step', and it is a lab prototype, not a deployed capability. My searches found no documented, independently reproduced, deployed LLM that learns continually in its own weights as of the evaluation date. The forecast stays open.
limitations: A broader reading of 'learn', such as in-context learning or developer retraining, could be argued to refute the claim already. That reading was rejected as stretching the claim against the speaker.
The search for 2026 deployments may have missed recent lab releases.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLMs cannot re-evaluate things and learn, and will never be able to do so.

statement.excerpt: We do not know how thinking works in humans and thus cannot extrapolate it to a machine, and at the very least human beings have the ability to re-evaluate things and learn, a thing that LLMs cannot do and will never do.
statement.document_title: How To Argue With An AI Booster

from_speaker: human beings have the ability to re-evaluate things and learn
a thing that LLMs cannot do
our_interpretation: The subject is LLMs themselves, the models. It is not wider systems that bolt on external memory, retrieval stores or prompt notes around a frozen model. Earlier reviewers said counting those would stretch the claim against him.

'Learn' means human-like learning after deployment: the model itself takes in new experience during use, keeps it, and revises earlier conclusions. Offline pre-training or periodic retraining by developers is not what he means.
'Will never' has no deadline. It cannot be confirmed within any finite period. It can only be refuted early by a decisive event.
criteria.support_condition: A forecast of 'never' cannot be confirmed on any finite record. At most, the evidence keeps showing that deployed LLMs do not learn from experience in their own weights.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A publicly documented, independently reproduced LLM that, in ordinary deployment, updates its own parameters from new experience, keeps what it learned, and revises earlier conclusions, without depending on external memory stores.

evidence.excerpt: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful but static; they lack mechanisms to adapt their weights in response to new tasks, knowledge, or examples.
evidence.explanation: Researchers describe standard LLMs as static, without built-in ways to adapt their weights. This matches the present-tense part of the claim at the time.

evidence.excerpt: Through supervised finetuning (SFT), these self-edits result in persistent weight updates, enabling lasting adaptation.
evidence.explanation: A research prototype shows an LLM steering its own lasting weight updates. The authors call it 'a promising step', not a deployed capability, so it is not a decisive refutation under the stated rule.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: An independently reproduced demonstration of a deployed LLM that keeps updating its own parameters from new experience during use, retains it without catastrophic forgetting, and revises earlier conclusions. That would contradict the claim. Nothing finite can confirm 'never'.
